findings.title: Reject missing cases while no already-seen tag/type is saturated
findings.mechanism: The new checker enforces first sample n=0, increasing unique IDs, class domains/caps and exact impact cardinality, but still permits missing samples that the C emitter necessarily emits. Point example: from the five-distinct-tags positive, drop n=1 (or n=2, or the last sample). Remaining samples are nonempty/increasing/in-range and all flags stay under counters, so they pass. With cap2, case1 must be sampled because at most one earlier case of its tag exists. Impact example: for five cases all type0 and cap4, replace sample IDs0,1,2,3 with0,2,3,4. Exact type0 cardinality4 and all current identity checks still pass, but case1 necessarily had to be sampled. The advertised complete sample set is therefore not yet enforced.
findings.bounded_correction: For each family track whether any already-observed tag/type has reached its quota. Before that happens, require contiguous case IDs with no gaps; the first min(case_count, quota) samples necessarily form a prefix. If the sample list ends before the case count and no class was saturated, reject the unfinished tail. Once a class is saturated, missing cases can legitimately belong to it, so do not invent unreported point-tag populations. Keep existing exact per-impact-type counts and per-class/domain/ordering checks.
findings.controls: Add real-script negatives dropping n1, a middle sample and the final sample before saturation; include the all-five-type0 ID replacement0,2,3,4. Add/retain positives with all-five-same-point-tag emitting only0,1 after saturation, one/zero cases, distributed tags/types, and existing binding/nonbinding caps. No RNG reimplementation is needed.
findings.evidence_level: Concrete source-path analysis of actual checker and emitter; no tests or Lua were executed by reviewer.

what_is_resolved: Per-family duplicate/descending/out-of-range IDs are rejected; point samples cannot follow impact samples. Tags0..5/types0..7 and per-class quotas are checked.
